newsitem.title: USA: Citicorp seen eyeing Latin America.
newsitem.headline: Citicorp seen eyeing Latin America.

text.p: If Citicorp decides to jump back into the acquisition arena, banking analysts believe its most likely move will be to buy a bank in Latin America.

Next to giant Citicorp, the second largest U.S. bank with $290 billion in assets, any acquisition would not be considered a huge deal based on the numbers. For one thing, banks in Latin America in general are not that big by comparison.

While U.S. investors have been burned many times over the years in Latin America, analysts said the image of the region is considerably improved in the last few years and acquisitions by foreign firms are more often than not viewed positively.

Raphael Soifer, analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman, noted that HSBC Holdings Plc announcement last week that it would purchase the Argentine financial group Roberts Group received a favorable reception in the market.

Jason Mollin, an analyst at Smith Barney Inc who specializes in Latin American banks, said Argentina is enjoying economic growth in the five to six percent range and this is likely to continue for the next three to five years.

He said the financial system in Argentina has a low penetration of the marketplace, for example less than half that in the United States. Boosting market penetration can leverage the growth that comes with an expanding economy.
According to recent reports in the Argentine press, Citicorp took a look at Banco Rio but in the end Spain's Banco Santander SA agreed to buy a 35 percent controlling stake.

Asked to comment on acquisition strategy, a spokesman for Citicorp said the company has looked at the privatizations that have taken place in Latin America. He said that would fit the company's strategy of making acquisitions that further its business objectives.
Citicorp chairman and chief executive John Reed -- who coincidentally grew up in Argentina -- has publicly talked about acquisitions in emerging markets, credit cards and money management.

George Salem, analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattison, agreed that "right now Latin America is enjoying a good image" with accelerating growth. But he wrote in a research report Friday that profibility in Citicorp's consumer banking business in the Asia-Pacific region is a problem. The analyst noted that Citicorp's 10-Q filing for the first quarter of 1997 referred to "moderating economic conditions" in the Asia-Pacfic region. The filing went beyond the language in the first quarter earnings report issued in mid-April.
Noting that Citicorp gets 12 to 15 percent of its earnings from consumer banking in the Asia-Pacfic region, Salem downgraded his rating to hold from buy.

Mandle said "not that many countries ... are suffering a slowdown in Asia" while some in Latin America are doing better. "On balance, the environment for their strategy is still pretty good," he said.

The decision last month to hire Peter Carman from Putnam Investment Management Inc to be chief investment officer was a clear signal that in investment management Citicorp has decided to build rather than buy, analysts said.

Asking prices of investment management companies that are for sale are considered too high to suit Citicorp. Carman will oversee investment management worldwide and is expected to begin building staff in the area.
Ronald Mandle, analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein Co, said he believes that in general Citicorp will do a deal provided it is "the right deal at the right price."
At the annual meeting in April, Reed confirmed that Citicorp and American Express Co has talked about a merger, but without going into detail he said nothing came of it.

There are few people in Wall Street who expect Citicorp to get involved in any show-stopping deal such as a tie-up with American Express. The rumor mill has even had Citicorp linked with brokerage giant Merrill Lynch & Co Inc.
Citicorp shares were off 5/8 to 113-3/4 Monday afternoon.
